utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Could we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As indicated yesterday, we have first of all to decide on the request of the Defence to admit into evidence two former statements of Witness O. The Trial Chamber decided not to admit these statements into evidence. But if the Defence so wants, the Trial Chamber will give a certificate in case of appeal because it's a principal question. The reasons for our decision are that we considered that witness evidence under our Rules of Procedure and Evidence is the live testimony of a witness in court, or alternatively, witness testimonies or statements under specific rules such as 71, 89 [F], and 92 bis. We also considered that the Trial Chamber of the Tribunal does not possess any knowledge as to the conditions, circumstances, and context in which a witness interview statement has been obtained and whether or not such statements were taken by legal experts of national or international authorities according to international recognised procedural standards. We have to consider that the witness' live testimony in reaction to being challenged by confrontation with former interview statements will represent the evidence, and that the witness interview statements only serves the purpose to aid in the challenge of specific parts of live testimony and do not by themselves represent such evidence. We also have to consider that the challenged part of the witness testimony is clearly reflected in the trial transcript and that it will be taken into account by the Chamber when making their findings. Therefore, it's up to the parties to take care that the special parts of a former statement will be reflected in the transcripts, and this can only be done by quoting an entire paragraph in the transcripts. In addition, it is true what the OTP contributed yesterday when referring to Article 90 [H]. Indirectly, one can conclude from this rule -- these rules on cross-examination that this is a place where the parties may, and have to, find out whether or not there was any discrepancy between formal statement and that what the witness said or the party believes he said during the examination before us. And therefore, it would be unfair vis-a-vis both the witness, being absent now, and unfair with respect to the trial itself, to come later, trying to identify possible contradictions between former statements and available transcripts. Whenever a party believes that it's necessary to find out such discrepancy, the only available space is the courtroom. And therefore, it is not possible to admit additional material into evidence. Not only to be said in addition, this would open Pandora's box starting with such statements. We would end by coming back to former transcripts and, no doubt, there will be discrepancies between that what a witness said five years ago, two years ago, and possibly today. The evaluation of such discrepancies is for the Chamber, if there are any such discrepancies. And therefore, we can only regard that what has been said in the courtroom and is transferred into the transcripts as evidence available for us when making our findings. As mentioned before, witness interview statements, therefore, also in future not covered by Rule 71 or 92 bis, notwithstanding if they were established by the Prosecutor's office or the Tribunal or local authority in the former Yugoslavia shall not be admitted into evidence unless, in extraordinary cases, the Chamber rules otherwise as it has been in the past in the example where there was a discrepancy, a formal discrepancy, when a witness evidently signed a statement only years after the statement was given. So far the reason for this decision. In case the Defence wants to appeal, the certification will be given. To turn to a second point of clarification: As regards the very, very difficult Rule 68 in connection with former transcripts, may I take the comments given yesterday by the Defence as such declaration that they withdraw formally their possible right that the OTP especially emphasises or highlights the parts of a former transcript as exculpatory material if only they have access to all former transcripts in case a witness has been heard in the past, in another case. And then it would be up to you to find out what you, yourself, regard as exculpatory. This is restricted, of course, only to the transcripts, and it's not in connection with additional material, for example, exhibits, mentioned in these documents. If the OTP has the impression that exhibits mentioned there may be exculpatory material, they have under Rule 68 also to disclose this material and, in doubt, on the request of the Defence. But as we have Rule 68, I understand that what was said yesterday by the Defence as a withdrawal of their right to be -- that the transcripts be specially marked. Is that correct, this understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Unfortunately, it is not. We would not like to waive our right to have the OTP, pursuant to Rule 68, highlight or show at least the page number or pagination within the transcripts where Rule 68 exculpatory material may be applicable to our client. If I did make that comment, it was said, perhaps, in haste. What I tried to emphasise was that perhaps the OTP and the Defence can get together and work through that to the extent that there were some exculpatory materials. We have always felt and insisted that Rule 68 is an obligation that must be complied with, and is a protection given to the accused in this case, as well as Defence counsel. So unfortunately, Your Honour, we would ask that the OTP does emphasise within the transcripts, as well as the other exhibits and documents the Court referenced, to identify that exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any observations from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Rule 68 actually requires in its English version that the Prosecution disclose to the Defence the existence of material known to the Prosecutor which tends to suggest, in a sense, or mitigate, guilt or the affect the credibility of witnesses. And throughout the history of this Tribunal in every other case that I'm aware of, providing the document to the Defence is sufficient to comply with Rule 68. I should say that there was some discrepancies between Trial Chambers as to whether or not the Prosecutor had to identify which documents were being provided pursuant to Rule 68 and which were not. And this Trial Chamber adopted the procedure which we agreed with from that date on one of our Pre-Trial Conferences all documents that were pure Rule 68 would be identified as such when provided to the Defence. But, not in this case or any case that I know, inform the Tribunal has it been a burden on the Prosecution to identify which areas of a document are -- would tend to indicate -- suggest innocence or mitigate guilt. The problems with doing that are two-fold. One is just resources. But secondly -- as we would have to find someone through and mark these up. But also it would create a tremendous opportunity for error on appeal. Because the Defence would say: "Here's a 70 page transcript, and in page 49, line 3, it wasn't identified as potentially mitigating of guilt, and we think it is. It's an issue on appeal." The Defence undoubtedly doing their duty, the Defence counsel are going to read the entire transcript. And I don't think it should be or the rule requires that the Prosecutor indicate, in any way, how a document or material suggests innocence or mitigates guilt. The rule only requires that the Prosecutor disclose to the Defence existence of the material known to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of these contributions given by the parties, the Trial Chamber hereby decides that it is, under Rule 68, sufficient if all the former transcripts are given as existing material under Rule 68 to the Defence, and it is not necessary to highlight special parts of this former transcript. As it was said before, this is not true for additional exhibits. They have to be highlighted and they have to be disclosed as existing material in the sphere of the Office of the Prosecutor, because the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the rationale of Rule 68 is to grant access for the Defence for material being in the sphere of the Office of the Prosecutor. And we believe that the Office of the Prosecutor has fulfilled the obligation by giving the entire transcript, and then the Defence may find out whether or not it's in part or in toto exculpatory in the sense of Rule 68. For the fundamental importance of this decision, the Trial Chamber is prepared to grant also, as regards this in case of an appeal the necessary certification. One third point of major concern is the protection of witnesses. Here, evidently, the parties are more close together, but we regard it as necessary to protect the private life of witnesses. It's in the interest of the witness that their private life is protected, and it's in the interest of justice that there is not another additional deterrent effect that a witness has, not only to testify in a dangerous situation, but in addition, has to be aware that he has to be -- that he will be or might be confronted with additional questions related only to his or her private life, being not relevant at all for the outcome of the case before us. If you have a comparative view on different European legal systems, you will find out that we have different approaches. In some countries, the duty to mention former incidents, sanctions, expires after five or ten years. In other countries, you have even the explicit right of a person being sanctioned, for example, in Germany, on a fine exceeding or being not higher than three months' income, that person may say "I have never got a sentence. There was no sanction at all." Even though the sanction was handed down yesterday. It's the protection of the private sphere of a witness as regards minor offences. And therefore, the Trial Chamber will, in future, allow only questions related to serious offences and to such offences having an impact on the credibility. For example, false testimony, forgery, fraud. But we would really ask both parties to refrain from asking intimidating questions to a witness. I think for today, there are enough preliminary remarks. Any observations from the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just have one more preliminary matter, very unrelated to Your Honours' remarks. And that is the Court asked us to have translated Document 50A and 50C, and these translations are now ready. We can hand those to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 50A and 50C?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: C being the French version. We had the original in B/C/S, 50B, and the English and French translations are now available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You tender this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections for the admission into evidence of the two translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: None other than those previously stated, if any, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then those documents are admitted into evidence as 50A and 50C. C for the French version. Anything else before we start hearing the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just in regards -- sorry. In regards to the next witness, this witness does have a pseudonym. We need to assign a pseudonym to him, please, Your Honours, and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be Witness P and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may return to one issue on the Court's third preliminary or administrative point, protection of witnesses, just to touch upon it, perhaps we can take some time later in the week on our scheduled Pre-Trial Conference to discuss it at length, is the Court or -- I have a couple of questions if I may. Is the Court also going to grant us the necessary certificate for appeal on this issue if we decide to address it at a later point? We haven't decided on any of the issues to be perfectly frank, but I'm not sure, just so that I understand it, if the Court is giving or willing to grant a certificate on that issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Here it's more or less a question in abstracto. The other two points were practical, related to events yesterday, to your request. And it was in concreto. I'm hesitant -- better said, we are hesitant to give a certification where there are some doubts on the admissibility already, because when there is not a concrete case before us, you may ask what is the prejudice? As I said in the beginning of the procedure, vis-a-vis, for example, the OTP when challenging the right of the accused to make a statement whenever he wants in the rules given during the Pre-Trial Conference. We also said that only when it will be the case that your client wants to make a statement, and he is, of course, still invited to make such statements if he so wants, only then there would be the attempt to appeal, and then we have to decide whether or not to give the certificate. And I would say in an appropriate case in the future, we should come back to this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have one issue, perhaps, for clarification related to this, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I recognise the reasoning behind the Court's ruling, and you know we accept it naturally, although respectfully, may raise an issue with it later. If the Court allows only serious offences, which jurisdiction and how would the Court like us to proceed if potential future witnesses are brought up and we do have information or material about it? And if I may just elaborate on it, for example, the Court lists three although not exclusive items, false testimony, forgery, and fraud as examples. But if, for example, this same witness O was asked in a prior trial about any offence such as the one that we attempted to touch upon, and he answered falsely, even though it may be a minor offence, and I don't know that it is or really don't want to comment on that, would we be able to, despite the fact that it was a minor offence, show that that was false testimony given before? Because, honestly, we feel the Defence and respectfully that we are being confined in our Defence, and we truly believe that a witness is going to lie about something insignificant and minor that only speculation will lead us to believe whether or not some of the more important and critical areas that he's called upon to testify, whether or not there's much truth or any truth to the testimony. We understand that ten years has passed, but for us even under Rule 68, the Prosecutor is obligated to give us information that may be exculpatory or may go to the credibility of the witnesses. We would like to know for them if they've done, because I know, in other jurisdictions that's what the Prosecutor does, look at the history of the various witnesses determine both their past and testimony. We haven't received any such on any witnesses. I don't know that the Prosecution endeavours to do anything like that, but we certainly believe that those issues, if the witness answers honestly and truthfully, we wouldn't go into the detail of the offence. Have you ever been charged, yes or no? What was the result of that charge? And he tells us honestly. In a situation where a witness denies because, perhaps, and I'm saying it respectfully to the witness that was just here, perhaps believing that we wouldn't have access to that information, it's easy for a witness to come and say: "I've never been charged for anything, major, minor or moderate-type level crimes and I have never been incarcerated or I have never committed forgery, false testimony, or fraud." So it's in those instances we would like some clarification, if we may. And if not, we will proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is a totally different problem. If you can find out or you believe that you can find out a discrepancy between that what a witness has said in the past and this issue was already -- formed already past part of a former interrogation or statement, and you want to prove that it was not true what a witness said in the past, this is a totally different problem. But our point is you should not start to go into details of the private life not relevant for the outcome of the case. So this is, I think, a quite clear distinction and it's in a way linked to the first issue we decided today. Whenever you want to find out an alleged distinction, an alleged discrepancy, then please quote once again to the record the entire paragraph of the previous statement that we can avoid the additional problems. I think this is now enough on this point. I see you nodding, and therefore we shouldn't hesitate to start with Witness P. Witness P, under 65 ter, number 87, with face distortion, and we have a very short summary telling us, once again, two hours, but already yesterday you indicated that it won't be enough. So probably when we have time, we can go through the entire list of the estimated time, that we can come to a realistic expectation on the envisaged time for the OTP's presentation until the end of July. While we are waiting, do you already know when we have the advantage of hearing the witnesses by videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'll try to have an answer for Your Honour by Friday's meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The witness is being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. You can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, my apologies that, for your protection, you will be addressed only with the name "Witness P" to avoid that your real name is mentioned in the courtroom. You understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, and the examination may start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, can you tell the Trial Chamber where you were born.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I was born in Kozarac, the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to school and grow up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I went to school in Hrnici four years, and then four years in Kozarac. That's elementary school. And the four years of the electrical engineering school in Prijedor. I have lived -- I lived in Kozarac, and that's where I grew up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- briefly describe to us Kozarac, the area, and what towns and villages it's made up of.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Kozarac is an area the size of 10 by 15 square kilometres. There are quite a few villages, Kamicani, Kozarusa, Susici, Brdjani, Babici, and then up until the border boundary between the Banja Luka and Prijedor municipalities, that's how far the Kozarac municipality extended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What municipality is Kozarac in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Kozarac belonged to the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a map I would like marked as an exhibit and displayed on the ELMO for the witness. It's entitled "Kozarac/Omarska overview," and for the record, the ERN number on the top right is 02166503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this will be S51. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then admitted into evidence as S51.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, we're going to -- if you look at the monitor, you should have the map displayed. Perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's very small. Perhaps we can zoom on it a bit. Is it possible to go any closer to the map on the ELMO? On the video? No, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, can you indicate on this map where Kozarac is? Perhaps you can turn to the map that's to your right and just point to it with a marker. There's a marker in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Kozarac is on the main road leading from Prijedor to Banja Luka, 12 kilometres from Prijedor in the direction of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, can you put on the map -- can you point to where your home was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Here, where there's this small village of Gutici, about a hundred metres further down from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's marked on the map, Gutici, just below Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were living in Kozarac in 1992 before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I don't know the exact data, but around 25.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the ethnicities of the people that lived in Kozarac? Can you give us an idea of the mix of ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: In the very centre of Kozarac and in some villages, 95 to 98 per cent of the population was Muslim. But around Kozarac, there were villages which were -- which had a majority Serb population. And also a small number of Ukrainians - Galijani, as they were called - they were scattered throughout the territory of the Kozarac area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe prior to the conflict in 1992, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of property and life did you have prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I had my own company. I was the only employee in that company. I had a trailer truck that I used for timber and for construction material. I had a house, a few acres of land, some large garages. So I was a self-employed financially independent person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your work, did you travel outside of the Prijedor municipality? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I mostly travelled to Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Krupa, Banja Luka, in the -- places in the vicinity. I was transporting timber to the various companies in the area. So I did travel in a wide area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend much time in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a person who closely followed political events prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, at one point, everybody was forced to follow these developments. That was in the period leading to these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you active politically yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you done military service when you were younger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1980 and 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, prior to the conflict, were you a member of any reserve force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The entire population of Kozarac at one point, between the takeover in Prijedor and the actual attack on Kozarac, were put on the list of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was done by Captain Sead Cirkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that in more detail very shortly. But prior to the takeover on the 30th of April, were you a member of any Territorial Defence, police reserve, any kind of military reserve or police unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Until that time, I had my wartime assignment in Banja Luka as a reserve driver in a tank unit. I was a truck driver, not a tank driver. And that was the last wartime assignment that I actually had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct -- can you explain to us, legally, did you have your residence outside of Prijedor? And if so, can you explain briefly why that was. Perhaps the map could remain because we'll come back to it shortly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Officially, I lived in Kozarac, but I did have an address -- another address in another municipality where also my company was registered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that done for tax purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, it was more favourable for tax purposes because the tax rate was different in other municipalities. It was lower than in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you actually spend your nights? Where did you sleep in 1992 before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I slept in my family home in Kozarac, if I happened to be there, because sometimes I would sleep in a hotel if I happened to be on the road, travelling. But mostly, I spent my nights in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, Witness P, were you married in 1992 or prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, I was married, both until 1992 and in the year of 1992 itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any children? And if so, can you tell us the years of birth of your children.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I had two children. One was born in 1987 and one in 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, can you tell the Judges what you knew up to 1992 about the name Milomir Stakic? Were you familiar with that name at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, at the multiparty elections that were held for the first time in the entire Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I know that he was the vice-president of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recall seeing him on TV or hearing him on radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you told me you would not recognise him if you saw him? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned about, at one point, everyone became aware of politics and to follow it. Can you tell us a little bit about the events and the atmosphere that led up to the takeover on the 30th of April. In particular, I think you have the perspective of being a person who travelled throughout the region, so tell us what your experience was throughout the region of the Bosnian Krajina in the events leading up to the takeover in Prijedor on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, the situation from the time when the takeover happened in Banja Luka and most of the towns in the Banja Luka region which followed, and everything was geared towards Banja Luka instead of Sarajevo. Banja Luka became the centre. Some payment transactions went to Serbia, so Sarajevo was totally left out of the loop. There were checkpoints manned by the army and by the police. Until that time, it was called the "Yugoslav People's Army" and when the takeover started to happen, then the red berets started appearing. Some different insignia were worn on uniforms. A tank would happen to -- would appear, and it was no longer olive-drab in colour but blue because now it belonged to the police. So there was this feeling that everything was under control. People's movements were followed. It was impossible to get into Banja Luka without passing through checkpoints, and the same thing went if you tried to exit from Banja Luka. Everything was controlled by the army and by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the army and the police," did these forces appear to be allied with any political group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, at a checkpoint, it was difficult to notice that on the spot. But on the radio, the politics affected people. General mobilisations were declared. People had -- all the people had to report to the military departments. So the people who manned the checkpoints who were armed at that time, they were subject to the politics that was present in the media campaigns. And at that time, all the information from the outside world, except from the information coming from Banja Luka, Prijedor, the radio stations there and the TV stations there, it was cut off. There were no other media present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about a takeover in Banja Luka and other municipalities. Who took over power? Was there any symbols that you saw or flags that were different than those that existed before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The Serbian tricolour flag appeared. At one point, it was flown everywhere. At one point, people started wearing the red berets, those manning the checkpoints at the access roads to Banja Luka, in Celinac, Manjaca, and from all other directions. Several uniformed people would stand there together, the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware on the 30th of April that there was a change in government or in authority in Prijedor? And if so, can you tell the Trial Chamber how you became aware of that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, the access to the town of Prijedor, all the Muslims who worked in Prijedor at that time had to get off the buses on the 30th of April. That happened in Orlovci, and they had to go back home, which means that they automatically lost their jobs. And it was quite clear that these people were no longer welcome in the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the takeover on the 30th of April, which person was the -- in the highest position in Prijedor, to your knowledge? Who had the top political position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Party of Democratic Action won the most votes on the 1992 elections. And it was entitled to select the president of the municipality, and that was Mr. Cehajic. He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who replaced Mr. Cehajic after the takeover on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, according to the stories that we heard after the liberation of Prijedor, from what the fighters for the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were saying, Mr. Stakic took over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened? How did life change for you and for others in the Kozarac area, your neighbours, after the takeover on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, we became prisoners. It became a ghetto in a territory, the telephone lines were cut off from the rest of the world. Physically, we were also cut off because all the roads were blocked. So we felt this insecurity. We felt that we were in some kind of a prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the -- on one day did you become aware of an attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, before the attack on Kozarac, allegedly there was an incident. It was on the radio that the -- a Serb military vehicle was attacked, that a man was killed, and that everybody had to come in and surrender. What happened in fact, there was an incident. I don't know who really got killed and how many people got killed. But at that time, the shelling of Hambarine began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the area of Kozarac? You said you lived close to Gutici. Is that correct? Am I pronouncing it correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your home near Gutici or from the area of Kozarac, could you see any of the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, at night, one could see the shells. Sometimes you would be able to hear it quite well, and sometimes you would see the tracer shells that would fall quite slowly. These were -- they had some kind of a parachute, and they would light up the entire area. They were fired either from mortars or from Howitzers. I'm not a military expert to really assess that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of that attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I think one day or two days before the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that the attack on Kozarac started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The 24th -- no. The 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what day of the week that was, the 24th of May when the attack began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, it was Sunday, as you said yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the attack on Kozarac, was there any announcements on the radio or other communication from authorities in Prijedor to the people in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The Serbian radio made some broadcast. The Crisis Staff, war staffs, various groups were asking for loyalty, asking for people to surrender their weapons, to surrender and to express their loyalty to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were all kinds of options, and there were contacts between the political leadership in Kozarac and political leadership in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few moments ago, when we were talking about whether you were a member of reserve, you said at one point everyone in Kozarac became a member of the BH army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what defence or armed forces were organised in Kozarac before the takeover on the 30th of April, and after the takeover on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: There were people who called themselves green berets, self-styled green berets. There was also a group of Kole's men. He was a criminal. Then also a group of Ramiz's men. Ramiz was also a man who had spent most of his life in prison. There was also a man who was expelled from Germany because of drug-related offences. They collected a small number of people around them, they walked around Kozarac armed, wearing green berets. This did not have any kind of political support of the official BH governments Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or authorities. People simply did it on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this have the support of a lot of people in Kozarac? What did the majority of people that you knew? Were they arming themselves and becoming members of armed groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, sometimes somebody would join such a group, either without a rifle or he would buy a rifle from the Serbian reservists passing through Kozarac and offering weapons for sale. So somebody would buy a rifle. But there was no general support. But on the other hand, there was no other option. If we complied with the Serbian -- with the Serb requests, we would have to take a rifle and fight against our fellow Muslims in Bihac, because that's where they would send us. There was no other solution. People didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The groups that you were talking about walking around Kozarac calling themselves green berets, was that prior to the takeover on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I think that up until that time, there was a very, very small number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us how this changed over time with the takeover on the 30th of April and the attack on Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, it was quite clear to us that such an attack would happen. In Kozarac, too, it was just a matter of time because the political solution offered by the politicians in Kozarac was not accepted by the people in Prijedor, which means that the other side did not want to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned at one point everyone became a member in Kozarac of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian army. Can you explain that to the Judges, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, the captain reservist of the former JNA had been dismissed from the army. He was jobless, and he came willy-nilly. "We are on the other side, and the other side is the army, BH army. We have some ammunition, some weapons," and then one of the policemen said jokingly: "Well, we can defend ourselves for five minutes because that's how much ammunition we had." Then the entire population from the ages 15, 16 onwards were put on those lists in villages. This happened in all the villages, in the streets. So there were groups, and there were 400 rifles, all in all, at the disposal of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a remark by a policeman about "we can defend ourselves for five minutes." Can you explain a little more about that remark and what value you give to it, whether you agree with it or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, for someone, 400 rifles was a lot because he was better informed about firing from machine-guns. On the basis of the number of guns, number of bullets, we could make calculation as to the speed, as to how many bullets could be fired from those guns. And we laughed when we heard that. He confronted us with the facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact what? Please just explain a little further. I think we all understand, but just to be clear on the record. How much ammunition was available?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I don't know the amount, but the policeman said that we could fire five minutes with the rifles. I suppose it was about a thousand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any, to your knowledge, any weapons such as Zoljas, hand-held rockets, in the possession of those who were defending Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I think that we have the wrong translation. If my learned friend can ask the witness again about the number of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In English, I can read what I heard. But probably in B/C/S, there was a mistake. Could you please repeat your question, and then we have it in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, there just was a small technical problem regarding your answer. If you can repeat it, I asked you how much ammunition was available.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the usher please go to the microphone of the witness and put on both of them, and a little bit louder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, sorry, but again, the question is how much ammunition was available to those defending Kozarac, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I don't know the number. The 400 rifles could fire that ammunition in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of other weapons such as Zoljas, hand-held rockets, being available to those defending Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: There were some Zoljas, which were bought from the reservists coming back from Croatia and sold in different cafes along the roads, although some of them could not really be operated because they had already been activated in the battlefields in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see the microphone went off again for some reason. Perhaps the witness is touching it without realising it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Witness P.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those defending Kozarac have Howitzers and artillery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any tanks or other armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether there was any military forces of the former JNA in the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: They were around Kozarac, Kozarac and Prijedor. They were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Kozarac, was there any attack from the people in Kozarac on Serbian positions or Serbian civilians, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, was there an ultimatum or an order communicated to the people in Kozarac regarding a -- some vehicles that were going to come through the road, through Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, over the radio or in some other way, I'm not sure, it was announced that a column of vehicles was to pass through the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road or the other way around. There was a checkpoint in Jakupovici another one in Kozarusa, Koncari. It was ordered that those checkpoints should be removed to a depth of a few hundred metres from the main road so that the column could pass without any problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it indicated that this was a column of army vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was said that a convoy of army vehicles was to pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the people in Kozarac who had set up the checkpoints or barricades respond to those radio announcements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Anyway, those checkpoints had been removed as was ordered, and the column was coming, one from Banja Luka, the other to Prijedor, and their aim was not -- their aim was not to go through Kozarac, but when they were approaching Kozarac, they started firing at the houses and the checkpoints, one could see at a depth of 100 or 200 metres with machine-guns from armoured vehicles, trucks, and shelling started from the nearby hills. On the civilian part of Kozarac, the houses there, the religious buildings, shells were falling all over the place. There was no particular order. When the people were in panic and started to the woods and the forest to find salvation there, the shells were fired at them, too, so they were returned -- they returned to the inhabited areas, to their homes, so that the population went around in circles without any particular aim and without knowing what to do. And not knowing what the solution was. No one felt secure. No one knew how to act. It was general chaos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this shelling, did it appear to be directed to any particular military position? Can you describe what was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, shelling was, in a general sense, everywhere. This lasted two or three days, until the 26th when it was ordered that the people had to leave the territory of Kozarac. Everyone had to leave to go to Prijedor to be able to mop up the terrain. I never heard this word before, cleaning the terrain. I heard about cleaning an area from garbage, but cleaning non-Serb population from the area of Kozarac is something that I hadn't heard before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This word that you hadn't heard before, can you tell us what that word is in your language, of course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, it was later known as ethnic cleansing, which was carried out all over Bosnia, wherever Serbs took over power, in different villages and places, and then we understood what that word actually meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the actual word used? Was it "ciscenje"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you first start hearing this word "ciscenje" around the time of these events that you're talking about in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, the term was heard even before that. But it was never used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the use of that word of cleansing to mean ethnic cleansing, who was using it in that sense? Was that the Muslim people that you knew, or was that the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian authorities cleansed the terrain of non-Serb residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. My question is, when you first started hearing the word, you said you first started using the word at this time used in this sense, who was using the word like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, when a military patrol came in front of our house and told us that we had to all leave to Prijedor because the terrain had to be cleansed. Then we were sort of confused by that term and how it was being used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the kinds of weapons or shells, to the best of your knowledge, that were used during the attack on Kozarac over those two or three days that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, first, the two military columns that were attacking Kozarac from two directions used carriers. On the carriers, there were heavy machine-guns, anti-aircraft guns, and they were used to fire at everything, at houses, at any other building, from the road given the range of these rifles. And there was the infantry, which followed the vehicles, a hundred metres from them. And everyone would run away, and then they would set fire to the houses in both directions from the side of Prijedor and from the side of Banja Luka. So that a great part of Jakupovici and Koncari was razed to the ground. And also, there was air fire from the launchers, from the neighbouring hills. So these were two parallel operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could turn to the map, S51, to your right and use the pointer, point out the areas that were under attack. And if you know, if you can, from where the attack was coming, or the attacks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, one column came from the direction of Banja Luka to Prijedor in the place of Kozarusa, and the other column from the place called Jakupovici. With the neighbouring Serbian villages, Babici, a part of the artillery was located in Tomasica, a part of the artillery was located on a hill in a place called Orlovci and artillery fire was going on from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there against the whole territory of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You circled an area of the map, and just so the transcript is clear, that circle went around Kozarac and extended as far north as Rakovici as, and as far south as Sivci and as far east as Kamicani, and as far west as Kozarusa? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Jakupovici -- Kozarusa, to the west, up to Jakupovici, up to the Trnopolje/Trnovo railroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see on our map, there are two Jakupovicis marked, one with the letter "G" Jakupovici and one "D" Jakupovici. Which of these do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Both places. Upper Jakupovici were taken over very quickly. This is the old road, Prijedor/Banja Luka. And here the army was stationed nearby, and so upper Jakupovici was taken over, and then they went in the direction of Kamicani using the old road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, on the map, there's a couple photographs marked numbers 11 and 10. Do you recognise those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Number 11 used to be a mosque in Kozarac called Mutnik. Number 10 is the church, Serbian church. It used to stand there, and it remains in Kozarac today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the mosque? Did that remain in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: What can be seen on the picture remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the mosque damaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: It was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that -- by the way, during this shelling that was going on for two or three days, was there any outgoing fire, outgoing rifle fire, weapons fire, from people defending Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I was never there on the outside lines. I heard that there was sporadic shooting leading to Kozarusa and Jakupovici. To how great was the extent of that firing, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you actually, you and your family, during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Home, in my family home in Gutici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate to have a break now. Then the trial stands adjourned until 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We may continue immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, can you tell us what happened at the end of the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: There was a mass exodus of the population in the direction of Prijedor, and we, from our garage and from our home, we went in the direction of Prijedor. We took an unusual route to Prijedor, an unusual direction, so that we arrived at the crossroads of Kozarac/Prijedor, from the south direction, south of Trnopolje, along with a convoy of vehicles consisting of several trucks, cars full of women and men. We came to the crossroads, Kozarac. At the crossroads, Kozarac --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, I want to come to that a bit later. I want to go back to the end of the attack. At some point did the shelling stop, or did it slow down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, in the meantime, in the days during the shelling, I went to the police station which was moved out of Kozarac and placed into a house under a hill. And I found out that it had been agreed that the population would surrender, that all would be surrendered and that a delegation from the police went to Prijedor. And there, it was to take us, some of the soldiers of the BH army to Prijedor. This wasn't done. The captain, the commander of the police in Kozarac, someone by the name of Osman, who was from Petrovac, he went to Prijedor for the second time, and he never returned. The people was very confused, what was happening, what about the surrender? No one was able to tell them, "you should go there." The people systematically went in the direction of Prijedor in large columns by foot. Some of them went to the highway from Kozarac, the other part of the people went from Kamicani, took the main way on foot. Many of them went from Susici to the main road, Kozarici, generally the population took the main road to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we discuss in more detail the exodus and your trip out of Kozarac, I think we need to cover a bit more in detail what you just talked to us about regarding the police station. This police station you went to, where was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: It was on the road Kozarac/Mrakovica, above Kozarac, 2 or 3 kilometres above Kozarac, at the foot of the hill almost. It was actually an abandoned hotel or motel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many policemen or other armed men were in the police station when you visited it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, all the policemen who could no longer work in Prijedor, until the takeover, were there and used to live in Kozarac. They were in the police station, and then the people who worked and lived in Kozarac earlier were there, too. There was a number of reserve policemen. I don't know the exact number. I can say there were about up to 15 active policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The policemen that you're talking about, were they all from one ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, they were, with the exception of one reserve policeman who was from the Ukraine, a Ukrainian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other reserve policemen, were they Muslim, Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, they were Bosnian Muslims. On the eve of the attack, there were those of other ethnicities, but they had disappeared that very night from amongst the ranks of the Kozarac police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These other ethnicities the night that the attack began on Kozarac Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, they withdrew to the Serb villages and they sided with the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at -- what happened after you came back from the police station? Before the exodus, before you actually left, tell us what led you to take your family and leave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I went through Kozarac. Some of the houses had already been destroyed and set on fire by the shells. I didn't go to the main intersection of Kozarac/Prijedor Road. I went using an auxiliary road to my street. And I assumed that the tank was already parked at the main intersection in Kozarac and that the army was already there. I came to my house, and I told the men standing in front of it that it seemed that the -- there was the surrender and that we had to go to Prijedor. They asked me why. I didn't know what to tell them and where to go. I didn't know what to tell them. A few minutes after I arrived, a military vehicle with two or three armed soldiers, who were unknown to me, came there and told us that we all had to go to Prijedor and that during the -- a few days' period, the cleanup of the terrain had to be conducted, and that then we would be able to go back. They didn't use force. They didn't discharge their weapons. They simply peacefully asked us whether there were any people in the houses further down from our houses. We said that there were. They went on. We went to our vehicles, to the tractors, and we went to the intersection on the access route to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "soldiers in a military vehicle" did you understand this to be a former JNA army vehicle, now the army of the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: It was a Jeep that was still painted in the former JNA colour. The insignia that the persons on the vehicle wore I didn't see. They mostly wore their hats either in their pockets or on their shoulder bands, so we couldn't tell what the unit was that they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you understand that to be a unit, part of the army that was attacking Kozarac, as opposed to being part of the Defence Forces for Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- the difference was there, because there were no such units armed in that manner and having that kind of vehicles in Kozarac, so it was quite clear that these were the troops that actually carried out the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the garage where you were staying, were there people besides your immediate family, your wife and children, staying with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: There were the children of my neighbours, people from villages quite far away, some people who had fled the upper Jakupovici had also found refuge there the night before, or maybe two nights before. They slept on the bare concrete floor. There were a lot of us, and it wasn't possible to provide any extra accommodation for these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the Jeep came by, what did you, and those who were staying with you, do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: We got into our vehicles, into the tractors, and headed towards Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What vehicle were you yourself using at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I was in my car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who travelled in your car with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: There was my wife, my two children, and a neighbour of ours, a woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning back to the map, S51, can you show us the direction that you took and the journey that you took when you fled your home near Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: If my house is here, below the village of Gutici, I had to go to this road here to the north. That was the main road. That was the route that I would have had to take. But we decided to take a circuitous route so approach Kozarac from the direction of Trnopolje, this intersection here. So we took a longer road, and we reached the intersection from the southern direction. That's the intersection here depicted on figure 3 here. So we approached the intersection from this direction. That was the convoy of vehicles approached the intersection from that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, could you take a marker -- I believe there's one in -- to your right; if not, you can use this pen -- and just draw a small box in the approximate location where your house was and put the letter "P" next to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said -- going back to the pointer, can you show us the -- perhaps you can use the marker. Draw with the marker the route that you took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, what about -- we are in open session. Indicating the house, I think shouldn't it be redacted from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think it's a large enough scale that the witness would -- is basically just indicating a village. But perhaps in the interests of caution, it should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Please, let's do it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the AV technician just informed me, it won't be shown on the public film, this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. This part where the witness just drew the box will not be shown on the public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, using the pointer, can you point again to the route that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you took and where you first stopped on your journey fleeing Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say you first went north up towards Kozarac, to the main road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Slightly to the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never went into Kozarac, you went south of Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No, to the south. We approached it from the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: From the intersection -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: At the intersection, we were met by a tank that was already standing there with a lot of troops wearing black uniforms, olive-drab uniforms, blue uniforms, camouflage uniforms, the blue ones belonged to the police. They started shouting at us. Why did we come from that direction? We said that we didn't know why we didn't come from any other direction, that this was the road that we took. They told us that we had to leave all the vehicles there, and that the men would be separated from the women, and that we would be bussed to another location. But since it was getting dark, the column from Kamicani on the main road was increasing in size, and the number of buses that was available for the transportation was too small. And an active police officer, I knew that man, in fact, managed to persuade this group of various troops that we should continue towards Prijedor on our own vehicles just the way that we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This intersection where you stopped, can you describe that? Did it have a name, or can you give it some description so we can be sure of what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: It was the intersection on the main road, Prijedor/Banja Luka main road. On one side, there was Kozarac, and on the other there was the road to Trnopolje. And there was a press, a printing press, on that road to Trnopolje a few hundred metres from the intersection. And in front of the printing press, there was a parking lot for the cars of the people who worked there. And there, on the parking lot, I saw some bodies in police uniforms lying around the parking lot to the right-hand side of the road and to the left-hand side of the road on the road leading to Kozarac. I recognised one of the men, the dead bodies, lying there. He was an active police officer. His last name was Klipic. His first name, I don't know. Sajidik or Sanidik, I really couldn't say. I knew him at any rate, because he was a strong man. He was slightly fat. And I could see his face. All the other police officers were lying on their faces, face down. Some of them had the active police officer uniforms and some had the reserve uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These police officers that you saw, you said that they were all in uniform. Could you tell or have any way of knowing the ethnicity of these deceased people that were lying by the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, according to the stories that I heard during my stay in the Trnopolje camp, a reserve police officer told me that when they approached the intersection in Kozarac, the whole group of people were put on a stadium in Kozarac, and the army or -- I don't know who it was, in fact, came to the stadium and told them that all police officers were to leave the group of people assembled there. My colleague, who was also a reserve police officer, he wasn't wearing his uniform, and he didn't want to leave. And when the police officers left the ranks of the people assembled there, they were taken from Kozarac in the direction of the main road leading from Prijedor to Banja Luka. The people assembled on the stadium were able to see that, because the stadium was right at the side of the road. And after a short period of time, there was a lot of shooting further down from the intersection, which is an indication that these men were killed there on the parking lot of this cardboard factory. In other words, that the group of police officers who had been taken away from the stadium, from the great mass of people assembled there, that's where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the one person that you recognised, the police officer whose -- the deceased police officer you recognised, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The recounting of events that you just told us about where the policemen were separated out of the stadium, who told you -- where did you learn this? Is it correct you told us you learned this while you were in the Trnopolje camp? I'm not asking you for the name of the person at this point. Just where did you learn this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: In the Trnopolje camp where I met this man who was himself on the stadium, together with the police officers who were taken away. And I saw them lying there scattered all over the place. So we simply put these two events together, and the -- it turned out that what I said and what he had said was, in fact, true, that these were the police officers and the reserve police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the police officers' uniforms distinct from army uniforms? Were they different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The police uniform was blue, and the military uniforms were of a dark colour, black or olive-drab or camouflage. So they used any colour but blue, but the police used only blue, either in a camouflage pattern or just plain blue, but it was always blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many corpses in the police blue uniforms did you see, to the best of your recollection today, in that parking lot along the side of the road there at the intersection where you first stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: At least ten dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in your group that came from the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact figure, but it was over a hundred people, in all kinds of tractors, vehicles, cars. Perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that other groups came from different directions. Is that correct? Can you, again, point on the map and indicate where these groups came from that met at this intersection. Sorry, you have to use the one to your right so we can see where you're pointing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: As we travelled from Gutici onwards, we went through a part of Hrnici, and a part of Suhi Brod. And cars and tractors joined our group with a lot of people so that the convoy increased in size and in length until the time when we reached the Kozarac intersection from the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did more groups continue to arrive at that intersection as the hours went by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: A large column came from Kamicani to the Kozarac intersection. And as they let us go on our vehicles to Prijedor, we could see this endless column heading towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of people were these? Were these men that appeared to be soldiers, young men of military age? What kind of people were in the convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: These were people of all ages. There were the elderly, the infirm, the disabled that were carried in wheelbarrows. So men, women, children, all the population from Kozarac was heading towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was everyone in a vehicle, or were there people on foot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Apart from our convoy that approach the intersection from the south, all the rest were on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the authorities from Prijedor, the SDS authorities from Prijedor, did they arrange any transportation for this group, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Transportation was organised by Autotransport from Prijedor and Rudnik Ljubija from Prijedor. These were the only two companies that had buses. Some other companies had buses for their own purposes, but all of these vehicles were used to transport people from Kozarac. Men were taken to one accommodation, and women and children were taken either to the sports hall in Prijedor, their families in Prijedor, or to the village of Trnopolje. But at any rate, this was organised. It was not just one bus. There were columns, lines of buses waiting for people to board them, for women, children, and men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at one point there were some places men were separated. When did that occur that men were separated from women, children, and others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: In Kozarac itself, men were separated from women. Then in Susici and in Kozarusa, they were again separated so that just a very, very few men, including our convoy, managed to get to Trnopolje with everybody on it. Because in other groups, men were taken away, separated from the women, children, and the elderly. Men were then taken to Keraterm. Some were taken to Brezicani, to a community hall or a school there. So that when we got to Trnopolje, the next day, we learned that these men were either in Brezicani or in Trnopolje, and also in Omarska. That people were already being taken from Brezicani and Keraterm to Omarska, to the buildings that were used by the iron ore mining company in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understanding that it would have been impossible for you to have counted, how many people would you estimate you saw during your flight from Kozarac that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: We're talking about people coming from two or three directions. At that time, I think we're talking about 10.000 people who were transported during that night either to Trnopolje or to Prijedor, Keraterm, Brezicani, Omarska. So during that night, most of the people were taken away. The greatest number of people were taken away that night, although it continued during the next two days, the 26th -- after the 26th. But at a smaller scale. During the first day, that is, in the night from the 26th to 27th, the largest number of people were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your trip to Trnopolje, did you see any houses or buildings destroyed in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: As we drove from Kozarac to a village further away from Kozarusa, that was the route that we took to Trnopolje using some local roads, from the main road, from what we could see from the main road, to the left and to the right, we saw a lot of houses that had been burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say -- first, I'd ask you to turn again to the map to your right and show us the route that you took and where you saw the burned-out houses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: This is where we got to the main road, and then we turned left to Prijedor. And in the village of Koncari, which is further down from Kozarusa, we took a local road lead to go Trnopolje. We were led that way by a police or a military vehicle. I'm not quite sure which vehicle took the lead there, because I was not at the head of the column. But from this place, from Kozarac to this place, we could see a lot of houses that had been burned down from the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say the houses were "burned down." Do you distinguish in your mind between how a house looks that was hit by a shell and a house that was burned? Do you have any information that they were hit by shells or burned by people setting fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Houses that had been hit by shells, in most cases, the shell would detonate inside the house. And the first thing that would happen would be for the window panes to fly out, and then it was not highly probable that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the house would burn down due to that. Most of the houses that I saw during my journey was blackened from the outside, which meant that they were either set on fire by incendiary rounds or using some kind of gasoline-based cocktails. I don't know what. But at any rate, the houses that were hit by shells, their roofs would not be burned totally. And houses that had been set on fire, their roofs would also be completely black, burnt. And that's how I was able to make the distinction between a how that was hit by a shell and a house that had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that many of the men were separated out, but that your group was allowed to go on to Trnopolje. Can you explain what happened and why you were not arrested that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The idea that I had, my assumption was that at that time, there was -- there were too many people coming in, and that it wasn't -- there weren't enough buses to take them away, and it was already getting dark. And that's why the decision was made to allow the convoy go through towards Prijedor, and then to take a shortcut, so to speak, to Trnopolje. And that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, we're talking about your smaller convoy of about a hundred people, you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The convoy that set off from my yard and the convoy that joined us enroute to the intersection. Perhaps we're again talking about a few more hundreds of people who had joined us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived at Trnopolje, and you spent a couple days in Trnopolje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the day -- the date that you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I arrived in Trnopolje on the 26th. In fact, on the night between the 26th and the 27th, very late that night. There was also a sports field next to a sports hall and a cinema hall and the school. It was guarded on all sides by the army. There was no way out for the men. Men could not leave that camp. We could move freely within the perimeter that was defined by the patrol points. The women and the elderly were able to go to Prijedor, provided they obtained a permit for it, they could go to their families or friends. Although, two or three days later, even that was banned, and then women and children were also unable to leave. At that time, a train, a cattle train, was set up, and many women and elderly were put on the cattle train and were taken to the territory controlled by the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say a "cattle train," what do you mean? Was this a train that was normally used to carry passengers? What do you mean by "cattle train"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: It was a train without any chairs, without any windows. There is a door, and when people are put in, the doors are closed, and it has a tin roof, a metal sheet roof. And the people have to survive the trip, several hundreds of kilometres, without any water, without enough air, in very hot weather, until they reach the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were at Trnopolje, going back to the burnt-out houses that you saw earlier, during the time you were in Trnopolje, did you see fires from where you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
