utterances.text: In the course of the -- during the night and during the day, since Trnopolje was slightly -- on slightly elevated ground, you could see flames and smoke from the houses burning. At that time, there was no shelling any more, which meant that this was done -- all done by hand, that houses were burnt by hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of accommodation did you receive in Trnopolje, you and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I did not seek accommodation. I slept in my car. Others slept in the school, in the gym, in the community hall. There were small tents or people slept under the trucks. Everything was full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people would you estimate were in Trnopolje during the days that you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: During the two days that I spent there, the number of people would increase. I estimate that there were between a thousand and 2.000 people. And if the place started to fill up, then the train would come and take away a certain number of women, children, elderly and disabled people, thus making room for new refugees that arrived in the course of the next two or three days, I mean arrived in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, you were told that Serbian authorities said that Trnopolje was a refugee centre, and that no one was detained there, they were there of their own free will and simply protected by the Serbian authorities, what would your reaction to that statement be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, if you had any brain, you would not be discussing this with any of the guards. I had my own opinion, and they had their own opinion. As far as I'm concerned, I felt that I was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any guns placed around the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, there were several machine-gun nests. There were well-armed points where people observed if anyone was trying to escape or approaching the camp. Everything was under control from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you recall, were the machine-guns pointed in any direction? Were they pointed out from the camp or in towards the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Towards the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The commander of the Trnopolje camp was someone, Kuruzovic, who was wearing a military uniform. His name was Kuruzovic. I don't know anything more about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of food was provided to you and your family in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: My family and I, we received no food during the two days I spent in Trnopolje. We had some reserve food from the car. During the day, a vehicle would come with a bit of milk in cartons, and a bit of bread, and this was distributed quickly amongst the people. And mostly, the women asked to be let -- to leave the camp, to go in search of food in the neighbouring houses in Trnopolje so as to provide food for people in the camp. There was no organised food provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you -- that you left the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, it was not my decision. It was the decision of other people. Some two brothers, some twins, who were drivers, messenger boys, they came with notes in their hands and looked for a number of people by name and surname. They said these people should follow them to be examined, questioned, in Omarska or in Keraterm. They didn't know exactly. They found me and another two acquaintances, and they took us to the Omarska camp where we were questioned on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on to the Omarska camp, I want to ask you a few more questions about Trnopolje. When you left Trnopolje, did other members of your family remain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: My wife remained another nine days after me. And my two brothers and father, they remained until the camp was closed down in Trnopolje. October 1st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your wife left after nine days. Do you know how she received permission to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The southern part of the road of the territory under the main road, below the main road, Prijedor/Banja Luka, was proclaimed a free zone, some kind of free zone. And all the people who lived at those addresses were able to leave the camp and take along with them some members of their family, friends, to their homes. And thus, my wife asked for such permission from the Trnopolje camp and took several members of her family and acquaintances to our home, and they remained there until July 10 or 11 when they -- all the people that were accommodated in my home were deported a day or two before Petrovdan, they were taken to Trnopolje, and then deported definitely from the territory of Prijedor. This was the last group of women and children and residents who were distributed in the different homes, houses, and 99 per cent of the cases Kozarac was abandoned. And those who were not in Trnopolje, they were taken and deported to Trnopolje and the other camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said your wife left about nine days after you were taken to Omarska, she went back to your home. What about your father and your brothers? Did they go with her, and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Men of an average age were not allowed to mix with the women, children, and the weak, and they remained there in Trnopolje until the camp was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people your wife had living at your house during the time between her release from Trnopolje and her expulsion from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, the house is a fairy large one. I think there were more than 50 people for that period of time of one month or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had your house, did your wife tell you, had your house been destroyed or damaged or looted in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, according -- when she left the house, the house was in a fairly good shape, with the exception of technical goods that had been taken out. The vehicles had been taken away, the spare parts, the fuel, the oil. On several occasions, several groups of soldiers of the Serbs, they were the ones who took those goods away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife attempt to bring any food to your father and brothers in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: During her stay in our house, she went either every day or at least every other day to take them some milk, because there was nothing else they had with the exception of some cows that they had caught in the meadows. They took them, and they milked them, and the only thing they could take was the milk and some dairy products, some cheese. So that she took care of them during their stay of one month in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it dangerous for your wife to go to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: It was dangerous. Any form of movement was dangerous. There were many drunk soldiers along the road who were not subject to any control or command. There were cases of rapes, women, of murders of people passing by. It was always a risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to the Omarska camp. Do we go to about 5.15, Your Honour, before the next break? Going on to the Omarska camp, and, Witness, I'm not going to ask you about all the conditions at Omarska. Let me begin by asking you, on the first day, were you interrogated while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived in Omarska, we were taken to the premises of the camp, that is to say, the iron ore mine. I had never been there before. They told us to wait in a corridor on the first floor. Then we found out this was the kitchen, that they were looking for premises where we could be interrogated. A large door was opened, and the two guards who escorted us to the Omarska camp, there I saw a very large group of people who were sitting around many tables in a large room. They were discussing about something. I don't know what the subject was. I recognised some Serbs amongst them who had been active police officers, reserve police officers, worked in the Criminal Investigation Department of the Prijedor police. And they said they had brought some criminals, and that some of these people had to interrogate them. The people from that room said that the door should be closed, and that they should wait and that three people would come to interrogate the three of us. And that is what happened. We were questioned that night, before that night. And we were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then placed in the premises of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your questioning, were you beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: During the interrogation, there was a civilian standing. I had to sit on a chair the wrong way around so that my back would be free for beatings. During the interrogation, there was a civilian standing behind me, and a young person in uniform was questioning me. The other one was taking down notes. He wasn't interfering in the conversation. And when the person interrogating was dissatisfied with my answer, then he would give a sign to the civilian to beat me with a rubber baton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything going on in the next room during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: At a given moment, we were silent. They were waiting for an answer. And I heard screams from the next room. It was my colleague who was also beaten at the time. His ribs had been fractured during the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about two specific incidents that you witnessed at the Omarska camp. Are you aware of a holiday that's celebrated among Serbian people on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: This holiday is called Petrovdan, Peter's Day, and they usually rejoice the night before. On the 11th, there was a lot of rejoicing, singing. This was what happened in times of peace when such holidays were celebrated. But on this occasion, also I must mention that fire, that fire -- there is fire also during that celebration. On that occasion, tyres are set fire to on that night. I don't know how this happened. Some were selected to go to the white house. During our stay, and according to the stories of those who had spent time in the Omarska camp, the white house meant death. A day or two was the maximum one would stay there. And then a group of people who were in the white house during the bonfire which was set -- the fire that was set as a bonfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so on the night of the 11th of July, did you see a fire set by camp guards celebrating the holiday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. We could see that from our room which was on the first floor of the building in which we were accommodated. If the guards were looking at us closely, we had to crouch. We were not allowed to look through the window because it was fairly low, up to let's say a metre. So there were some holes, however, through the tin, and we could see what was happening. Not everything, but we could see people move, and we could hear the screams and the shrieks of the drunk guards, the songs, the shooting, whether it was -- whether people were targeted or not, we do not know. We had a picture of what was going on in front of the white building and the bonfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you looked out, do you recall seeing one particular incident around the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, I saw a concrete incident when a person, a man, was pushed into the fire. People started shrieking and yelping. And a person who was standing next to me and sitting next to me, he said that this was a family of the captain of our army, Cirkic. I don't know if this is true or not. I don't know if it was about that person. But I can say that I had seen the person disappear in the fire, and then I escaped from that window. I no longer watched what was going on, and my colleague told me that at least ten people on that night ended in that bonfire, and the big truck tyres had been set fire to and who had been selected for the white house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see one man in the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: He was pushed into the flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you yourself couldn't recognise the person, but someone next to you told you a name. Did you know the person that he had named?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: By name, I didn't know him personally. But when he said that he was the brother of the captain, then I knew who he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Had you seen that person -- this is the brother of Captain Cirkin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Cirkic. Cirkic's brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the first name of this person who was in the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know this Cirkic well enough to know -- to recognise him if you saw him? My question is: Did you see him after that day and if you could have recognised him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: His neighbours, who said that it was about him, he told me that he was not there and that no one had ever seen him after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He told you that this Cirkic was never seen after the fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: That's correct. And this is true even now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going on to the next incident, do you recall some men from Hambarine arriving at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. A group of -- a larger group of people, perhaps 200 persons, two or three busloads of people, and they were accommodated in all the buildings of the camp. The camp was fairly full at the time. There were about three or three and a half thousand people in the camp at that moment. Once these people were accommodated, then the guards came to the doors again and said "all the people who have entered the rooms a few minutes before, that they should leave those rooms and should go to some other place." Most of the people went out, and they were accommodated in the white house allegedly for further transportation. This was being said in front of the door. Nothing happened in particular until the moment, 2.00 or 3.00 at night when I was woken up by shots fired by pistol. I got up slowly and looked through the window. And next to some lemon tree, which was fairly high, I could see many dead people. Some were alive, though, who were lying in a circle around the white house, in front of the white house, in the direction of the red house. So these people were lying around, and the guards who were on duty on that night went to -- from one person to another, and they would shoot another shot in the head of the persons who were lying on the ground. This lasted for a -- until they had visited all those people, and everyone was given an extra bullet that was shot in their heads. After the end of this shooting, a truck was started which was parked in the lower part of the building. Then loading truck was also parked and also started. They came in front of the white house. They took a few prisoners from amongst the people who were sleeping in what we called -- a premise called the hangar. They had to load these people on to the truck, and the truck would four or five times throw -- it was an like an excavator. The people were loaded on to the truck. This was done four or five times. Then they were taken somewhere, and then the truck would return. I didn't count how many rounds were made. I think there were at least four or five truckloads of times. And then the truck had to be cleaned because of the blood that was there. I don't know which people were there until I arrived at Manjaca. Then a person said that these were people from Hambarine, that he, too, had been in that group. But when the people were ordered to leave the premises again, he didn't want to leave. He remained, and that is how he survived. And that the group that was with him was liquidated on that night and taken somewhere else. And in the neighbourhood, in the vicinity of the camp, because the truck didn't stay away for a long time after having driven the group of people that were loaded on to it. On that occasion, I heard from -- I recognised from one of the guards, Marmat, Zivko, was his name, who went along with that group of guards and who was shooting a bullet in the heads of the people who were lying around in a circle around the white house and around the red building, too, in the field around the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us an approximate date or at least the month when you witnessed these killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The killings took place on July 16th and 17th, very early in the morning, 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. Everything has already been done, so the people getting up in the morning were not able to see what had been going on previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the bodies were loaded first into an excavator. Is that the type of machinery with a very large shovel in the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they were put on to a truck. Can you describe the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was a FAP truck of the 1921 type which had a volume of about 8 to 9 cubic metres. And the excavator was a Radoje Dakic excavator. The shovel was about 2 cubic metres, so four or five people could fit into that shovel which was then lifted and then loaded on to the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon the bodies that you saw behind the white house and the number of loads put on to the trucks that you observed, do you have any estimate of how many people were killed that night? Are we talking about 10, 20? Can you give us some estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: My estimate would be about 180 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time for a break. Could we break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we begin, just one thing occurred to me: Is it possible to redact? In the beginning of the witness's testimony, I asked him for his year of birth, and he gave the exact date. And I would suggest in a public transcript that that be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It may be redacted. Unfortunately, it's too late, the 30 minutes have expired, but on the version to be distributed, it shall be redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us about two killings you witnessed in Omarska, one involving Petrovdan, and the other one the 16th, 17th of June, that night. Were you aware of other killings that happened in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: As for the disappearance of people from the camp, let me put it that way, I do know about many such cases, although the Tribunal is not really very interested in me speaking about these incidents except to mention the names of the persons who were taken away from some rooms and never -- to the white house and never came back. And indeed, have never been seen since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I briefly interrupt. Of course, this Tribunal is interested, and please feel free to say whatever you want also spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a quick comment on the record. Just for clarification, I think when my learned friend the Prosecution asked on the date of some of the killings, he mentioned the month of June. It was my recollection, although I haven't scrolled back it was July the witness was referencing. With all due respect, if you could just clarify that, and let me know what it is, that would be fine. Sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, I want to emphasise and invite the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness whenever he wants to express, he may do so spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, the events that I was talking about, the murder, the killing of people from Hambarine, took place in July, 16th and the 7th of July. So just to clear that up. As for the other killings, I can mention the killing of Jasmin Hrnic, Eno Alic, and Emir Karabasic, who was also an active police officer from Kozarac. They were killed in front of our rooms in a large hall. All the rooms on the first floor could hear -- everybody in those rooms could hear these people being tortured and the way that they were killed. And later on, they disappeared on that day from those rooms in the camp. That is as regards those three people. And I can also mention some other people who were also taken away in the same way and never came back. I don't know where they were taken to. I would really like these people to be alive here, and it would be easier for me if I could say sorry. There was Vasif Kahrimanovic who had a sawmill, Enver -- Ekrem Melkic. I will mention some drivers such as Mehmed Hodzic, nicknamed Medo, a driver that worked in the mine -- Ljubija mine. Hare Dautovic, he used to be the manager's driver, chauffeur. Then a cafe owner, Sivac Sefik. He was beaten up and killed. I saw his dead body lying next to a hedge near the red house. This is what I saw as we went -- or rather, ran to the kitchen where we had to line up. And then at one point, we were able to run to the kitchen, eat there, and then come back to the -- stand next to the wall, and we were able to see some bodies lying next to the hedge. And Sefik Sivac, who was one the owner of one of the cafes was also there. And many of the active police officers who were held in the Omarska camp were taken away to be exchanged as they called it. The exchanges never materialized, and these people never came back, were never since. There's Hamdija Arifagic. He was a police officer. Then also Senad Sarajlic, who was also a police officer. Alic, Esad, a police officer. Kevljanin, a man whose first name, I don't know. He was a police officer. Ismet Taras from Ljubija, police officer. And I think only one or two active police officers, in fact, survived. One of them had a mixed marriage, and also my physical education teacher. And the other one survived by mere chance. All the other active police officers were killed, and so were many of the reserve police officers including their commander Osman, who disappeared on the first day when Kozarac fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you saw a body by the hedge. I believe you said that was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I saw Sefik Sivac's body next to the hedge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other bodies besides Sefik Sivac's body, other bodies while you were in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Frequently during the day, people who died due to the beatings, the injuries that they sustained or due to natural causes would be deposited next to the hedge, and then the next night they would be taken away somewhere in an unknown direction. At least, at that time we didn't know where they were taken to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone by the name of Dr. Jusuf Pasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I do know him. He was a general practitioner in Kozarac, and he was also the director of the clinic in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Omarska camp, and do you know what his fate was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I saw him in the Omarska camp. They were held in a room close to the kitchen. He was taken away, together with a large group of intellectuals. There were also Dr. Eso Sadikovic, a lot of managers from various companies, people who were politically active. And they were taken away on one occasion from Omarska, and their fate remains unknown to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know someone named Mirsad Alisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I knew Mirsad Alisic. He was with me in the same room. And he was taken away in that group of people that included also Dr. Pasic and I think also Mr. Cehajic, the president of the municipality, was also there. But people were shouting: "Listen to these lists, to the names of these lists. It's -- now the time has come for the intellectuals to be taken away."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Alisic's position, profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I think he was an inspector in the criminal investigations division in the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned on this particular occasion there was a list. Was it common for the guards and the personnel at Omarska to have lists of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: In the first days when the camp was set up, the investigation centre as they called it, when it was set up, there were no lists. But then one day, on our way back from the kitchen, everybody had to supply their personal details to one of the guards who noted down all the information into a big book. And every room had its own book, and if somebody, a guard or somebody who had anything against anyone, if they came looking for somebody, they would know from these books where that person is. And they would really make an effort to find that person and to abuse that person, beat him. Or even on some occasions, even so assist that person. All kinds of things happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the camp personnel, the guards, inspectors, and others, actually look at your identification? Did they take information from identification that you were carrying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: When I came, I had to show my ID card for the purpose of interrogation, so I was registered by the interrogation commission. And they had the proper information for the people. And most of the people had to show their ID if they had any ID.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about many of the people that you knew are missing from the Omarska camp. Did you notice any pattern or any criteria for the selection of those people who were particularly targeted for abuse or for killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: All the people who had any money were in a high-risk group, because various groups of people took an interest in them. It was their task to collect the money from the prisoners. All the people who were politically active were also on the lists for the white house where they were subjected to beatings and all kinds of special treatment including their being put in the white house and also their eventual disappearance. Also, the police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about professional people and those who were highly educated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Those people were held in a room next to the kitchen, and most of the people from that group were in that room next to the kitchen. And a part of people that were housed in some other rooms, they were taken away one afternoon and their fate remains unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know someone named Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. He was my physics teacher in the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Medunjanin or any members of his family in the camp, and do you know, if so, what their fate was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin was beaten in the camp, and he died as a result of his injuries and the blows that he took. He died in the white house. On one occasion, as we came back from lunch, I saw him lying close to the white house. He was still showing signs life. He was taken and brought in that afternoon, and then we knew nothing about him. Safeta Medunjanin [as interpreted], his wife, was taken to an exchange. The exchange never took place. Her bones were found in a communal grave between Sanski Most and Bosanska Krupa. So that also speaks to the fact that the group in which Medunjanin's wife, Safeta Medunjanin [as interpreted], was, that its fate was really the worst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the first name that you're using for the wife. Can you tell us, is that Safeta with an F, or Saneta, with an N?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I think her name is Sadeta?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With a D? The third letter is D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. Another woman who had been politically active, a wife of a dentist, Velida -- I can't recall her last name -- met the same fate in the Omarska camp. She disappeared in unknown circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose any weight while you were in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: During my stay in the camp, we were given one meal a day. If we were in the last group, in most cases, we would get nothing to eat that day. We were given a piece of bread for the day and some really very thin gruel, cabbage soup. In two and a half months, I lost almost 30 kilos in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you weighed when you got to the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Not upon our arrival, but when the international organisations, the Medecins Sans Frontieres and the Red Cross when they registered us, we were weighed. And on that occasion, I weighed 46 kilos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your approximate weight before you went to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Around 75, 76 kilos. That was my weight before I came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, during the night, we were taken to the Manjaca camp on the buses of the Prijedor transport company, Autoprevoz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I want to return for one last question on Omarska. Did you see how the bodies were removed of those who were killed in Omarska besides the one night you talked about involving the people from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: If we were awake early in the morning, we were able to see a small truck. That was driven by Serb guards or uniformed workers. They would load the few bodies, four or five bodies, on to it, and they would take them away before most of the people woke up. But at any rate, we didn't sleep really well, so everybody was awake at any given time. And a lot of things were observed. We could hear vehicles coming in and going out, and this small vehicle was used to transport the dead bodies from the hedge, which is quite close to the red house that I had already described, very early in the morning in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about your trip to Manjaca. Take your time, and please describe to the Judges what happened, what that trip was like, your trip from Omarska to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: In the camp itself, I mean in Omarska, we were divided into groups, three groups. We didn't know where each group was going to, but at any rate, we were divided. Later on, it turned out that a group remained in Omarska for a week or two after we had left. Another group was taken to Trnopolje. And my group had to go to the Manjaca camp. We were put on to buses, about a thousand and five hundred people. I don't know how many buses there were exactly. I think there were about 20 of the buses. We all had to, during the trip, not at first, but during the long part of the trip, the last part of the trip, we all had to go to the back of the bus. We all had to lie on our stomachs, and we were not allowed to look out of the window to see where we were going and what was being done. The guards sat in the front of the bus, the drivers drove the buses very slowly. And during the trip, some people were called out by their full name. Among others, Dedo Crnalic, a well-known tailor from Prijedor was called out, but he did not respond to the calls from the people who were looking for him. As we passed through the Serb villages Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. such as the villages enroute to Manjaca, the buses would stop in front of cafes or on the road. People would get out drunk out of the cafes and hit us, spit on us, shouting various slogans, singing songs. Some of them of nationalist nature so that I felt that the trip lasted for an eternity. It may have been about a hundred kilometres, but it lasted for a long time. When we got in front of the Manjaca camp, the commander of the camp, a captain -- in fact, I don't know his exact rank. He didn't allow the people to get into the camp during the night when the lights were on. He said that everybody had to spend the night on the buses, and then when the day broke, that people would be taken into the camp where they would be examined by doctors, where their personal identification documents would be taken away, when they would be registered. And only then could they enter the camp alive. During that night, my bus, the people -- my group on the bus had to make room for the guards who slept on the bus while the other guards stood guard around the buses on a large meadow, an open space in front of the barracks, or rather the camp, because the camp itself was a set of barns that had been used for cattle. And that's where we were housed the next day. The next day, when we got up and when we were separated from the people from the other buses, we had to sit in a valley, and the people who escorted the buses, the guards -- I don't know what term to use -- came there, and picked out a few people from the great mass of people that was there, took them away to a place not far from us. These people were killed. I don't know how they were killed, but I do know that one of the guards who was engaged with Dedo Crnalic, who was dealing with Dedo Crnalic, wiped his bloody knife against his shirt -- Dedo Crnalic's shirt, and he came to us whether he asked us that he knew whether Manjaca was the largest Serb village in Yugoslavia. Nobody said anything to these words, to what this soldier said. He then said that Tito had destroyed the village and had set up the farm there, and the largest tank training area in Yugoslavia. He said that the village would once again become the biggest Serb village in Yugoslavia, and he said: "We will expel all of you and liquidate all of you who wanted to destroy Serbs in this area." After these men were killed quite close to us, the camp commander saw himself that something was going on. He didn't want to leave the camp itself. He said that the dead bodies -- that he refused to accept the dead bodies into the camp, so the dead men were loaded on to the buses that were returning to Banja Luka empty. And then from there, to Prijedor. According to what we heard in the Manjaca camp and on the basis of the information from Banja Luka that reached us one way or another, the dead people were found in the Vrbas River, caught in a dam or nets that were placed in front of a hydro electric plant near Jajce, so they were thrown into the river. We were registered and allowed to enter the barns in the Manjaca camp. It happened that day. Our transfer to the camp itself took almost the whole day. In the camp, we found four barns that were already full of people from other municipalities such as Kljuc, Sanski Most, Doboj, so that at the time when the six barns were full of people, there were about 4.000 people in the camp, prisoners, I mean. Until the final closing down of the camp in December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions about the trip before we go to Manjaca briefly. What was the temperature like on the buses during that trip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I forgot to tell you that the heating on the buses was on, turned up to the maximum, although during the summer you would usually -- you would usually turn it down. And one of the men on my bus, Kemal Jakupovic, in fact, died because of the intense heat on the way to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided with water or food during the journey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: We didn't get anything during the trip until we entered the Manjaca camp. That was the first time that we were given any water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that were escorting you, the guards, do you know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: These were people I didn't know, but according to the stories of people from Prijedor or the town of Prijedor, it appeared that these were people from Prijedor, who used to live in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing army or police uniforms, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Dedo Crnalic. I may be mispronouncing his last name. Just to be clear, was he killed that night or that morning when you arrived in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: On that morning, before we entered the camp, he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he was a well-known tailor. Why was Dedo Crnalic well known?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: He had a very modern shop, one of the first boutiques that appeared in the region. He owned such a boutique in Prijedor. He was a rich man. He was good at his job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained in Manjaca, can you tell us approximately how many people, if you have any idea, were from Prijedor municipality that were detained there, or what percentage of the prisoners were from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: You mean from the municipality? Well, about a thousand five hundred people from Omarska came, and all this were people from the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were released in December. Was your release facilitated by any organisation, any international organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Our release was organised by the Red Cross, the Association of Refugees, the UNHCR, Doctors without Borders, and other organisations that used to visit us and that cared for us, brought food for us and medicine for us during our stay at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your release, do you recall if you had to sign any documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I remember very well. I signed a document. I don't know what I signed. The people from the foreign countries, they said: "It's not important what you're signing. Sign it. You're going to be released, and that's the most important thing." Now, what these documents were all about, I really don't know. I'm sure that everyone signed such a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your release and those who were released with you, where were you taken? Were you taken to the territory controlled by the Bosnian and Herzegovinian army, or were you taken to a third country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, one of the conditions for our release from the Manjaca camp, that we should leave the territory of ex-Yugoslavia, which in fact means that all those countries accepted a certain number of refugees along with their families. This was the condition put by the Serb authorities for us to be released, that is, to leave the borders of the former Yugoslavia in a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime later, you were reunited with your wife and family and children. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your wife and other family members, did you learn -- you told us about what happened to her and when she was released or put on a train out of Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, can you mention again the date that she was transported out of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I think it was on the day of Petrovdan and passing the border area which was under Serbian control, and then there was much commotion why the convoy was passing through on a holiday. It hadn't been announced. And they were being told of this during the trip, which, in fact, implies that they were deported on July 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your father and your brothers? Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: About their fate, well, I only learned about that when I left the camp and when I reached Karlovac. It was then that we found out that they had been released about October 1st, and we had been released a month and a half later through different organisations. Then we were able to contact them and my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until October, from the attack on Kozarac until October, were they detained in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. They were in that camp, in Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we began your testimony, you described some of the property and lifestyle that you had. And you mentioned, for example, also in your testimony that you drove a car to the Trnopolje camp. What happened to that car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: That car, a few days after I left for Manjaca, that car was seized by some people. And then later on, my brother had to sign a document in the name of my wife, because the car was owned by my wife, that he was giving the car in the name of my wife to Puhalic Slavko from Cirkin Polje for further use. An employee from Prijedor came, who dealt in such business, who saw to the signing of these papers, and this was taken to the camp where my brother signed this. He was not allowed to refuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, this document indicating that your brother had given away the car to this man, did you give that to the Tribunal, and did you see a copy of it today before you testified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I gave a copy of that document to the Tribunal. I have the original at home. And today, I looked at it again. It was signed by Mr. Slavko Puhalic. His address is on that document. Information about him, his ID number, and all the rest that was required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the name of the person that received this generous gift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. And that car -- well, I saw it quite often at the Omarska camp. What it was doing there, who was driving it there, I never saw it in motion. I saw it very often parked in front of the kitchen near some water where some of the prisoners had to wash it while it was at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that asked to have the car donated by your brother, who asked for the car, do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. He was a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him before, or did your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I didn't know him. I think my brother didn't know either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you had your own business, and I believe you said you owned a truck. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your truck during the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: During the conflict, my truck was parked in front of the Lignosper factory in Bosanski Novi. And until then, until the war days, I could always park the car on the premises of the company. And the last time, we were ordered that the trucks could no longer remain within the premises of the company, but that they had to be left on a public parking area. When the conflict -- when the attack on Kozarac began, these trucks were taken by the army, and they were driven to Prijedor, Banja Luka later on, so that I was able to see my truck on several occasions in Manjaca. I could see that it was transporting heating wood for the bakery in Banja Luka from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had a family house outside of Kozarac. What happened Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: After my wife had left the house, the house was looted. The roof, the windows, the furniture, the floor, all this had been taken. Also, the garage and everything that was in the garage. And this was the situation which lasted until 1995, until refugees from Croatia, Serbs who sought refuge from Croatia moved in. Mr. Mile Martic had given the house to refugees. They were given building material to repair those houses, and these people lived there until last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Martic, you're speaking of the former president of the Republika Srpska Krajina that was set up in Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. When Krajina, the SAO, MAO, I don't know what its exact name was, disappeared from the territory of Croatia, all the Serbs from there moved into Bosnia and Kozarac was -- the intention was to build Knin in Kozarac. The names of the roads were renamed to names of Knin streets. Then, Martic moved away from his refugees in search of greater business possibilities in Serbia. I believe that he has reached the Tribunal now so that his Knin on the territory of Kozarac failed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We want to move back to this case. Sir, after Dayton, after the peace, did you ever return to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, in 1997 was the first time I went to Kozarac. And there, I found the people that were living in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Kozarac look like when you went back in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Only the houses that were populated by refugees, Serb refugees, were in a fairly good shape. But the other houses that had not been populated and no one was living in them did not exist. This was organised by the Serb authorities in Prijedor who began to collect old iron, and the refugees had to take this iron from concrete and to sell it in Prijedor to be able to buy themselves food. And they also bought copper from the cables, building blocks, construction blocks so with the aim of destroying everything that had not been destroyed until then, until 1995, 1996, 1997. So that this was the second phase of destruction of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any mosques left in Kozarac when you went back in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Well, of the 16 mosques that had existed in Kozarac, there was not a single mosque that was intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, you've told us over the past several hours about many things that you witnessed leading up to the conflict, the attack on Kozarac, your experiences at Trnopolje, Omarska, and Manjaca, and the convoys that were organised to take people out of Prijedor. From your perspective of a person who was there during those events, did these appear to you to be random events, or did they seem connected to you, in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The deportation, rounding of people, taking them to camps, interrogation, liquidation of people, all that was very well organised. Who organised that, I cannot say. These are not things that could have happened accidentally at the time. To my mind, this came from a higher level municipal republican state. It was something that had been designed at that level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to have a purpose behind it, as far as what did they intend to accomplish through these destructions of the mosques, the houses, the detentions, the killings, and the deportations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: My idea was that all the non-Serb population should be expelled from the territory that the Serbs thought should belong to them, and those territories they thought of connecting up to form a greater Serbia, parts of Bosnia, parts of Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, this is my vision of that war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness P.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Two, more or less, technical questions: The witness said a few minutes before that he had given a document on the seizure of the car to the Tribunal. Could the OTP please provide us with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like a copy? The original is in evidence. Actually, I believe he indicated he gave us a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He said he had the original at home and provided the Tribunal with a document. And I believe it goes without saying that it is for all the parties as well, and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a group of documents here. I know the witness can identify which one -- they are all in B/C/S -- he is talking about. Perhaps the usher can give the witness the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first page of the document is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would the registry please present the document first to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the actual document that Defence counsel is looking at which they should also have in the proofing binder that they got with this witness, this document has some writing on it that's put on by the people that prepare the proofing binding, that do the all-systems search. There is another copy we could print which would not have that extra writing. It would be the copy of the document as presented by the witness. I stand corrected. The Defence did not get a copy of this document. I also haven't seen which documents the witness selected. If I could just have them, I could also read into the record the ERN numbers. Apparently the witness selected -- there are two pages, and it's ERN number 00174177 and 4178. Also, if the Court is going to use this, this should be marked confidential because it has the witness's name on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And there is -- the writing on the top, as I mentioned, is not part of the document. If the Court wants to accept this simply with that understanding, that's fine. Otherwise, we could provide a clean copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we should take the document as it is and take it confidential for the protection of the witness. And we have it in the record for the better understanding that something was added later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, to be clear, the writing at the top that's added begins "Selection of Personal Identification" and it's three lines and ends with pages -- it lists the page numbers, 1 to 6, 9, 13, 15, 17. That is added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is the understanding that this document is tendered by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd be happy to do that if Your Honours would find it helpful. To be honest, I didn't tender this simply because it would require translation into two languages and the basics would be covered by the witness's testimony. I didn't think the document itself was at issue. But if it would be helpful to the Trial Chamber, I would be happy to offer it into evidence. It is part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore, it's provisionally marked S52B. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Not at this time, Your Honour. But if we could be provided with a copy of it as well. And tomorrow in due course, we may or may not. But it doesn't look like it at this point, at least provisionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we decide on the admission of this piece tomorrow. But I think it would be only fair if the examination-in-chief would not be concluded without touching upon the document S51 once more connected with the question what comes into the mind of Witness P when seeing the sights on this document? Because there must be some intention from the side of the OTP providing us with these photographs not yet mentioned until now 1 to 9. As recollected correctly, we discussed only 10 and 11, and numerous places, not only Omarska, were mentioned by the witness. And I think it would only be fair that the witness has the possibility to tell us what comes to his mind when seeing these photographs. Therefore, it may be put on the ELMO once again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P, you discussed pictures 10 and 11. Can you go through the photographs starting at the photograph labelled number 1 on the left-hand side of S51, and tell us whether you recognise the photograph, and if so, what is depicted in those photographs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: This is the police station in Kozarac which was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about photograph 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Photograph number 2 is the railway station in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that railway station used during the transport of people, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: People were deported from this railway station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about photograph number 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Photograph number 3 shows the regional Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, the intersection in Kozarac, and this road here leads from Trnopolje. This building here is the sawmill in Kozarac, and that's all I can see on this picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the intersection where you saw the bodies of the policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: No. Before this intersection, from the direction of Trnopolje, perhaps 150 metres away from this place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What about photograph number 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Photograph number 4 depicts the building of the mine in Omarska where we were located. This is the kitchen, the white house, the red house, and the building where the people were housed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about photograph number 5?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: The photograph number 5 shows a view from an airplane, or an aerial view of a youth settlement called Benkovac, a youth camp which was on the Kozara mountain just a few kilometres down from the Kozara mountaintop which was also above Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the -- this Benkovac used for at the time of the conflict, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Before the conflict, the army was stationed there ostensibly for the purpose of a drill of some kind or an exercise. But the exercise never took place. The war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time that Kozarac was attacked, was this an army barracks, to your knowledge, or army camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes. It was used by the Serb forces withdrawing in the few months before the conflict from Croatia. They didn't go to Serbia as they were supposed to. They were deployed in various locations in Croatia, and one of those areas was Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Benkovac depicted on the map in the northeasterly area of the map, the last blue dot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Yes, in the right hand part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about photograph number 6? Do you recognise what's depicted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where this photograph was taken from. It was taken from an airplane or from a helicopter. It shows the wider area of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about photograph number 7? Do you recognise this? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: This is the TV transmitter Lisina, which was also shifted in such a way that it could only receive Serb programmes, Serbian programmes, after the takeover in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that transmitter in relation to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: If you head towards Banja Luka from Kozarac, it was at a distance of about 10 kilometres, and then you turn left again for some 10 or 15 kilometres to the top of the Kozara mountain. That is the highest point in the area, and that's where the transmitter was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise photograph number 8, what's depicted there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: This is the Trnopolje camp, the school in Trnopolje. This here is a large hall. This is where a shop used to be here on the corner. And this is where the people were housed, in these premises here, in a compound here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, you indicated as the area where people were housed, there appears to be a road running horizontally across the photograph at about the middle. Was that one of the boundaries for people of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Between this road and -- actually, on this meadow, this is where the machine-gun placements were so that people could never reach the road. That's the southern road leading to Prijedor from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise photograph number 9?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: Photograph number 9 depicts the hospital in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that was damaged during the shelling or the attack following the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P
utterances.text: It was destroyed later, and it hasn't been repaired and is not in use at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can it be agreed that we take this document in the form it has now with the additional remark where the house of the Witness P is located as in a method we used before, as S51P, and this be treated confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Court is referring to this document we just went over. Correct? I have no objection to it. My only comment, if the Court can assist us, on some of the pictures, namely, 1, 2, 3, 11, 10, and 9, there seems to be a date on the bottom right-hand corner. I don't know that the witness can identify the date. I certainly can't. And perhaps the OTP would be kind enough to provide us with the dates. Pictures 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, which are aerial shots, do not seem to have those dates. Or they can clarify to us if they do or not, so I don't have to ask the witness because I certainly can't make that out. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can help. I know the witness cannot help. But I can tell counsel that the witness who I expect can provide that information is Mr. Anayat [phoen], the team leader for this investigation. And he will testify and can provide counsel with that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to conclude, this document in the form of a copy including the mark prepared by the witness is admitted into evidence as S51P. The remaining decision on 52 will follow tomorrow. I don't think it's appropriate to start the cross-examination today. Therefore, I want to ask you, Witness P, tomorrow to hear and answer the questions of the Defence counsel and, of course, also questions put forward by the Judges. Thank you for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I ask the Court, perhaps ask the Court if it wants to ask to the admonition today, because the next witness is also present, ask the witness not to communicate with the next witness regarding his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you hear the request from the counsel of the Office of the Prosecutor, and do you agree not to communicate with anybody regarding your testimony of today until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this understanding. Any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then hereby we conclude this session, and we meet tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 6.54 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
